extracted.intended_audience: precollege mathematics teachers and curriculum developers
extracted.subtask_description: Catalog of mathematical 'habits of mind' (proof, geometric and algebraic approaches, ways of reasoning) intended to inform curriculum and instruction in school mathematics. Describes specific practices, habits, and illustrative examples that teachers can use to develop students' mathematical thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof and explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof establishes logical connections among statements; proof and explanation can be used to enhance an investigation in at least two ways: (1) Proof establishes logical connections between what you want and what you know; (2) the connections that a proof makes give you the feeling of explaining your result and suggest new theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and examples: do not start from first principles but connect desired results to known facts (example: deriving 'if p is prime and p divides ab then p divides a or p divides b' via the gcd as a linear combination). Use proof not as an 'add-on' but integrated into investigation — developing a proof alongside exploratory work often yields stronger, more general results (cake-cutting problem: show solution generalizes to shapes with an inscribed circle). Proof suggests new problems and sharper results; proofs should be checkable and convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as integral to investigation (not ritual/add-on)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof is not an 'add-on' that gets written after a result; it is an integral part of the investigation and the construction of the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop proofs alongside exploration and mental experimentation; doing so often lets you say more (generalizations) than the initial solution indicated. Curriculum implication: integrate proof development into problem solving rather than treating it as a ritualistic appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians push the language
rubrics_metrics.description: The drive to make results apply in new situations leads mathematicians to push definitions and the language of mathematics so concepts apply more broadly (e.g., expanding rules for exponents, inventing complex numbers, assuming existence to reach contradictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and examples: introduce and adjust definitions to capture useful generalizations, assume existence of undesirable objects to derive contradictions, and be willing to invent or extend objects (like p-adic integers or negative exponents) to gain new insights. Use examples (Pascal's triangle generalizations, extending cosine to vectors) to show how pushing language yields fruitful theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians use intellectual chants (rumination/rehearsal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Working mathematicians alternate between logical calculation and ruminative mental rehearsal — repeating lines of attack and ideas many times; these rehearsals sometimes produce breakthroughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical suggestion: include short descriptions of ruminations that occur during problem solving, interviews with reflective students, or ask students to reflect and write about how they approached a problem to build this path to productive mental activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric approaches provide insight across branches
rubrics_metrics.description: The geometric point of view has provided insight and has been an absolute necessity in many branches of mathematics; geometers have a particular collection of techniques useful across areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage geometric visualization and geometric heuristics; show historical examples where geometric thinking unlocked problems from other domains (complex analysis, p-adic geometry analogies). Use pictures, models, and multiple representations to support geometric insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometers use proportional reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole family of geometers treat real numbers as ratios of magnitudes and rely on proportional reasoning (dilations, scale factors, constant ratios) as a central tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dynamic tools (software that allows dilations) and measure-boxes to help students visualize changing lengths that maintain ratios. Emphasize proportionality as a bridge between numeric and geometric languages and as a necessary ingredient in vector methods and fractal geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometers use several languages at once
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometers often use multiple 'languages' simultaneously in an investigation (analytic/co-ordinate, algebraic, vector, complex numbers, turtle geometry, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to translate among representations (geometric diagrams, coordinates, algebraic expressions, complex numbers) and to appreciate that multiple points of view can be used in the same problem; classroom tasks should encourage switching among languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometers use one language for everything (geometric language generalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometers sometimes recast diverse phenomena in a single geometric language (points, lines, angles, planes), extending geometric concepts to novel domains to gain coherence and insight (e.g., interpreting tuples as points/vectors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how familiar geometric definitions (e.g., cosine) can be extended algebraically to higher/generalized contexts, and use that unified language to transfer geometric facts to nontraditional settings (e.g., geometry of vectors, p-adic geometric analogies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometers love systems (systematizing and unification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometers enjoy defining systems (geometries) and pushing analogies to see how far classical theorems hold in new finite or exotic systems; they also combine many special cases into one large result by viewing families of events together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to define their own systems (finite geometries, toy models) and to explore which classical theorems survive; look for unifying statements that cover many special cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometers worry about things that change (continuity/dynamics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because geometry developed to describe space, geometers reason by continuity and are interested in how things change; dynamic geometry software can support this habit and the development of conjectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dynamic geometry tools (Geometer’s Sketchpad, Cabri) to let students manipulate figures, observe continuous variation, and form conjectures (e.g., varying a segment in a trapezoid to locate an average). Emphasize experimenting with motion and limits as a route to new theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometers worry about things that do not change (invariants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Searching for invariants — properties that are preserved under transformations — is a key geometric habit (e.g., finding a point that does not move under a transformation, defining well-defined functions like the power of a point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach invariant-based reasoning: look for quantities or properties preserved by transformations, use invariants to show constructions are well-defined, and discuss examples from transformation groups, topology, and eigenvalues to illustrate the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometers love shapes (classification, analysis, representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The study of shape includes classification (congruence, topological properties), analysis (regularity, symmetry), and representation (models, drawings, computer graphics); geometers frequently use pictures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include tasks that classify shapes by combinatorial/topological features, analyze symmetry/packing/dissection, and produce multiple representations (drawings, models, computer graphics). Use visual materials heavily in instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraists like a good calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraists value calculations (with binary operations) and view computations as central; calculations are often performed not just with numbers but with objects (permutations, functions) for particular purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize purposeful calculation: represent processes (like a card shuffle) algebraically (permutations, cycle graphs) to reveal structure (e.g., that a permutation T satisfies T^12 = identity). Use calculations to build intuition and to motivate abstract structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraists use abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstraction is a central tool: algebraists abstract common features of systems to create new structures (groups, rings) that capture essential behavior and allow general reasoning (e.g., working with exponents modulo n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to extract the underlying structure from examples (roots of unity leading to cyclic groups), create new symbolic systems, and use abstraction to extend algorithms and theorems to broader contexts. Show how abstraction simplifies repeated reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraists like algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebra began as a search for algorithms: recipes for solving classes of problems. Algebraic algorithms can be recursive/inductive (Euclidean algorithm), produce shortcuts, or capture extensive calculations in a compact form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on algorithmic thinking: present recursive/inductive definitions, show concrete algorithms (Euclidean gcd algorithm, building matrices to test common roots of polynomials), and have students design/implement algorithms for algebraic tasks (counting combinations, iterating polynomial transforms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraists break things into parts (decomposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraists seek decomposition theorems that express complex objects as combinations of simpler 'building blocks' (fundamental theorem of arithmetic, decomposition of vector spaces or finite commutative groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach decomposition as a strategy: factor integers into primes, decompose vector spaces into subspaces, and use equivalence relations and classes to simplify structures. Use decomposition theorems as tools for counting, classification, and constructing algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraists extend things (work in larger systems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraists gain insight by embedding a system into a larger one to see how objects/theorems behave under extension (e.g., embedding integers into Gaussian integers to study primes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extensions strategically: show how problematic elements may be 'removed' by working modulo something or in an extension; examine behavior of objects (primes, theorems) under extension and use simple arithmetic tests to decide phenomena (e.g., splitting of primes modulo 4).
